source.title: Resolving superposition in AI for interpretability and cross-modal alignment in patient-neuronal images
source.authors: Jisung Park; Seohyeon Kang; D. Yoo; Eunsu Lee; Seoin Cho; Wooyeop Choi; Янлим Чой; J. Evan; Daesoo Kim; Sonia Gandhi; Minee L. Choi

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. There is minor OCR/formatting noise, but it does not prevent extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests superposition and its resolution in a trained image CNN using gated sparse autoencoders, feature-map interpretation, and representation measurements rather than the original neuron-visualization method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CNN feature maps co-activating for mitochondria and lysosomes, SAE feature maps separating biological concepts, and measurements across SAE dictionary sizes and sparsity penalties. Downstream geometry and cell-death prediction results are not included as rows because they do not directly measure neuron polysemanticity. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study's own result (Fig. 4a) shows channels of a custom image CNN co-activating for distinct organelles. This is a qualitative V1 observation in a new setting, microscopy rather than natural images. Everything else assumes superposition (theory with m>d posited) and reports properties and performance of the study's own SAE tool, so V3 and V5 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that superposition in bottlenecked CNN representations both mixes concepts and corrupts latent metric geometry, and that SAEs disentangle concepts and restore geometric fidelity with little loss of accuracy. They also claim that purified SAE vectors enable scRNA-seq-style analyses and de novo GW-map alignment with transcriptomic data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses gated sparse autoencoders trained on spatial feature vectors from a custom biological-image CNN, with dictionary-size and sparsity sweeps and biological-map validation; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported inner products and other SAE properties vary with dictionary size and sparsity penalty; at dictionary size 8192, lambda 800, the inner product rises relative to dictionary size 4096.

fits_no_version.finding: Gated SAEs trained on CNN stage5_out vectors give decoder directions with lower mean inner product (0.052–0.104 vs 0.160 for a small SAE proxy). They also give higher eRank and more class-specific features (697 vs 40). Probe accuracy stays within about 2 points of the CNN (88.23–89.91% vs 90.31%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc SAE decomposition of image-CNN activations yields lower-interference, more concept-specific features than the CNN's channels at small predictive cost.

record.problems: Evidence is from one custom CNN and one biological image setting. The polysemanticity examples are qualitative and representative rather than an exhaustive count of CNN neurons or feature maps. Table 1 values have no stated uncertainty, and the largest tested dictionary size shows a rebound in inner product.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream cell-death prediction, local-dispersion, Moran’s I, and transcriptomic-alignment results (Sections 4.3–6 and Figures 5–7) were left out because they assess downstream representation utility or geometry rather than directly measuring polysemanticity. Figure 4(b)’s mutation-specific feature-map counts were also left out because they do not measure mixed-concept activation.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 and natural-image classifiers. Prevalence of polysemantic channels, since only representative maps are shown. Whether the mixed concepts are truly unrelated.
Superposition as cause is assumed: the theory posits m>d. Feature count is never compared with neuron count, and capacity is never varied in the CNN itself.
No change to the CNN's activation, architecture or regularization. The SAE is post-hoc, so the share of polysemantic neurons in the model is never altered or measured.
Not examined, though the SAE colocalization feature hints that some co-activation reflects a shared spatial feature.
Not examined. Maps are thresholded at the 50th percentile with no comparison of thresholds.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-linked V3 and V5. Those rows report the study's own SAE tool (decoder inner products, eRank, probe accuracy), not tests of whether neurons are polysemantic because of superposition, nor of model architecture or training changes. Only the qualitative Fig. 4a observation bears on a version (V1). Preprint; one custom CNN; no uncertainty on Table 1.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses a custom CNN on neuronal microscopy images; it does not test InceptionV1, cat faces, car fronts, or the prevalence of such mixtures across image classifiers.
Transformer language models, MLP neurons, and token or context responses.

The paper argues for capacity pressure and varies SAE dictionary size and sparsity, but does not directly establish that the number of ground-truth features exceeds the CNN’s neuron count or isolate capacity pressure as the cause experimentally.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is sufficient capacity.
It tests SAE dictionary size and sparsity in one custom CNN setup, not SoLU, other activation functions, modern convolutional architectures, or a broad architecture comparison.
The study does not test whether the CNN’s mixed activations share a single underlying feature or job, or whether better interpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons makes unrelated mixtures rare.
It does not systematically vary the activation range examined or compare alternative explanation-scoring methods to test measurement dependence.

rows.measure: Whether individual feature maps co-activate across distinct biological concepts
rows.value: The paper states that conventional CNN feature maps polysemantically co-activate across distinct concepts, including simultaneous activation for mitochondria and lysosomes.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a qualitative result; it does not report a prevalence across all CNN feature maps.
rows.check: Correct link, but the evidence is representative images only, with no count or prevalence. Mitochondria and lysosomes colocalize spatially, and the SAE found a 'mitochondria-lysosome colocalization' feature (App. F.3), so the mixture may not be fully 'unrelated'.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Custom contrastive ResNet-style CNN (stage5_out channels) on iPSC-neuron fluorescence microscopy
labels.reason: Sec 4.2 and Fig. 4a: individual CNN feature maps fire for both mitochondria and lysosomes (R1). The evidence is qualitative, from representative images, with no prevalence.

relation.reason: Only the Fig. 4a observation tests V1, and only qualitatively. The paper mainly uses superposition as a premise for its SAE method, so this is a weak but acceptable test.

tranche.reason: New setting (a CNN on fluorescence microscopy). The study's own Fig. 4a and Sec 4.2 show CNN feature maps co-activating for distinct organelles, which is a result on V1. The rest of the paper assumes superposition and evaluates SAEs.

source_check.notes: The evidence is a single qualitative example (Fig. 4a) with no prevalence. Mitochondria and lysosomes colocalize perinuclearly, and the SAE has a mito-lysosome colocalization feature, so 'unrelated' is weak. The model is a supervised-contrastive classifier, not a self-supervised one.

statements.problem: None for this study. It is a custom residual CNN (stage5_out, 512 channels) on iPSC-derived cortical neuron fluorescence images, and its feature maps co-activate for mitochondria and lysosomes (Sec 4.2, Fig 4a). It gives no count. Preprint with code, seeds and SD, and a linear-probe capability check.

statements.correction: Custom residual CNN trained with supervised contrastive learning (SupCon with MoCo) on class labels for four-class classification (healthy control vs SNCA x3, LRRK2, GBA). Linear probe accuracy 90.31 +/- 0.38%. Inputs are fluorescence microscopy of iPSC-derived cortical neurons, not natural images.
statements.problem: The statement lists this study among vision models that are not classifiers. The text says the CNN was trained with supervised contrastive learning (SupCon+MoCo) for four-class classification and evaluated by linear probe. What differs from V1 is the image domain (microscopy), not the task.
